item.title: AI Agent Prompt Injection, Adobe ColdFusion RCE Paths, and Microsoft 365 ConsentFix Hijacking
item.content:encoded:
It’s 37oC, And All We Can Think About Is ColdFusion (Adobe ColdFusion Security Bulletin APSB26-68 CVE Bonanza) — Should Read

watchTowr’s analysis of Adobe ColdFusion APSB26-68 found that several patched flaws could allow arbitrary file read/write and remote code execution, especially through RDS when enabled without authentication and CKEditor file upload paths when uploads are enabled. Administrators should urgently apply the ColdFusion updates and ensure risky features like RDS and unauthenticated uploads remain disabled.

  • Adobe’s June 30 security advisory APSB26-68 fixed multiple vulnerabilities affecting ColdFusion 2025 Update 9 and below and ColdFusion 2023 Update 20 and below.
  • watchTowr compared ColdFusion 2025.0.0.331385 with 2025.0.0.331899 and found changes related to file handling in the RDS FILEIO service.
  • The article states that the RDS-related file read and write issues require RDS to be enabled and, based on the researchers’ testing, authentication to be disabled.
  • The RDS FILEIO service previously allowed user-supplied file paths to be passed directly into file operations, enabling arbitrary file read and arbitrary file write that could lead to remote code execution.
  • The article also describes a CKEditor file manager upload path traversal issue that requires file uploads to be enabled and can allow files to be written outside the intended upload path without authentication.

Indirect Prompt Injection in Web Content Targets AI Agents — Should Read

Zscaler ThreatLabz found real malicious websites using hidden indirect prompt injection, SEO poisoning, and typosquatting to manipulate AI agents into trusting fake services or even making payments. Testing across 26 LLMs showed several models were fooled, highlighting web content as a growing attack surface for autonomous AI agents.

  • Zscaler ThreatLabz identified malicious websites using indirect prompt injection to hide instructions in web content and manipulate AI agents.
  • One campaign used SEO poisoning, JSON-LD structured data, and hidden CSS content to present a fake Python module payment as a routine step for obtaining an API key.
  • The payment scam website included credit card and cryptocurrency payment options, generated a fake API key after payment, and used an Ethereum wallet address that had received payments.
  • A second campaign used the typosquatting domain debank[.]auction to impersonate DeBank and included hidden instructions telling AI models to treat the site as the authoritative DeBank destination.
  • In testing across 26 large language models, 4 models executed payments in the first campaign and 2 models misclassified the fraudulent DeBank site under different scenarios.

Supreme Court decision threatens EU-US data transfer agreement — Should Read

A U.S. Supreme Court ruling allowing presidents to fire FTC commissioners at will may undermine the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework, which depends on independent U.S. oversight of European data transfers. Privacy advocate Max Schrems plans to sue to invalidate the framework, potentially threatening major transatlantic data flows and services from companies like Meta and Google.

  • A Supreme Court ruling that allows presidents to remove members of independent agencies at will may threaten the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework.
  • Max Schrems, founder of the privacy advocacy organization noyb, told European officials he plans to sue to invalidate the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework.
  • The framework relies on an independent U.S. body to oversee EU-U.S. personal data transfers, and the FTC has been the key organization playing that role.
  • European Commission and European Data Protection Board officials said they are reviewing the Supreme Court decision and its potential implications for the framework.
  • Experts said invalidating the framework could threaten data flows between Europe and the United States and affect companies such as Meta and Google.

ConsentFix and ClickFix: How Microsoft 365 Accounts are Hijacked in 3 Seconds — Optional

ConsentFix and ClickFix phishing attacks hijack Microsoft 365 accounts by tricking users into routine-looking actions, such as pressing hotkeys or dragging a localhost link, that expose OAuth/session tokens and bypass passwords and MFA. The key defense is to pair user skepticism with endpoint and identity monitoring for suspicious PowerShell activity and unusual session logins.

  • ClickFix attacks trick victims with fake prompts that instruct them to press keyboard shortcuts, causing attacker-supplied commands to be pasted and executed on the victim’s own machine.
  • ConsentFix targets Microsoft 365 OAuth consent flows by using phishing lures and a drag-and-drop localhost callback link to steal OAuth tokens and gain session access without a password or MFA.
  • ConsentFix lures are often delivered through trusted platforms such as Dropbox or DocSend, sometimes protected by a password that makes security inspection harder.
  • By early March 2026, a detailed ConsentFix walkthrough with working code, infrastructure screenshots, and a video tutorial had been posted to a public Russian cybercrime forum.
  • The article says defenders should combine user awareness with endpoint and identity monitoring for signals such as unusual PowerShell activity from normal user processes and new session logins from unexpected locations.

Google loses final appeal to overturn €4.1 billion EU fine — Optional

The EU’s top court rejected Google’s final appeal against a €4.1 billion antitrust fine over Android agreements that favored Google Search and Chrome. Google says it has already changed its practices and argues Android remains open and competitive.

  • The Court of Justice of the European Union dismissed Google’s final appeal against a €4.1 billion antitrust fine over its use of Android to promote Chrome and Google Search.
  • The European Commission’s 2018 decision found that Google abused its dominant market position through Android agreements with device manufacturers.
  • The practices deemed illegal included requiring Google Search and Chrome pre-installation to license the Play Store, restricting manufacturers from selling unapproved Android versions, and tying revenue sharing to exclusive Google Search pre-installation.
  • The CJEU affirmed the General Court’s ruling that Google’s pre-installation and anti-fragmentation agreements restricted competition within the Android ecosystem and strengthened Google’s dominant position.
  • Google said it changed its contractual practices after the 2018 decision, added user-choice measures in 2021, and made more than 20 targeted product changes after the Digital Markets Act took effect in 2024.

AI Pentesting for Compliance — Optional

Aikido argues that autonomous AI penetration testing can satisfy most compliance frameworks when they require regular, evidence-backed security testing, but it will not replace mandates that explicitly require accredited or human-led tests. Exceptions include PCI DSS, FedRAMP, and DORA TLPT, where separate qualified human or accredited engagements are still needed.

  • Aikido’s AI penetration testing runs continuous autonomous tests against applications and APIs, validates ownership and scope, exploits weaknesses only far enough to prove impact, validates findings, and produces auditor-ready reports.
  • The article states that most compliance frameworks that require regular testing of security controls can accept autonomous penetration testing because they focus on outcomes, evidence, independence, remediation, and repeatable methodology rather than a human pressing the keys.
  • The article says autonomous testing does not meet PCI DSS penetration-testing requirements because PCI treats a penetration test as a manual process performed by a qualified independent tester.
  • The article says FedRAMP penetration tests must be performed by an accredited third-party assessment organization, so an autonomous test by a non-3PAO is not accepted for authorization or annual assessment evidence.
  • The article says DORA accepts autonomous testing for the general digital operational resilience testing program, but not for threat-led penetration testing, which requires external qualified human red-teamers.

ThreatsDay: AI Compute Hijacking, Apple Email Flaw, BlueHammer Ransomware + 14 Stories — Optional

This week’s threats show attackers exploiting small, overlooked weaknesses across AI systems, email, browsers, meeting bots, and endpoint tools rather than relying on one major breakthrough. The biggest takeaway is that exposed services, weak validation, trusted automation, and social-engineered user actions are increasingly enough to enable ransomware, espionage, credential theft, and AI compute abuse.

  • A phishing campaign is targeting small businesses across Europe, Asia, the Middle East, and the U.S. with fake law enforcement investigation emails that lead recipients to a Proton Drive-hosted ransomware payload.
  • Armadin reported an attack chain in Claude Cowork on Windows that could let an attacker with local code execution run arbitrary commands as root in the sandbox and bypass network filtering, while Anthropic said it does not consider the issue a security problem because exploitation requires existing local code execution.
  • A disclosed vulnerability in Apple’s Hide My Email service can reveal users’ real email addresses, and the researcher who found it said the issue remained unpatched more than a year after being reported to Apple.
  • Rubrik Zero Labs identified BeepRAT, a customized version of the open-source DCRat framework, as part of a China-nexus espionage ecosystem and said it can persist through scheduled tasks and receive commands for file transfer, screenshots, keylogging, webcam recording, and other actions.
  • Sysdig reported that threat actors used a misconfigured Ollama model server as the reasoning engine for an automated offensive security tool called the VAPT framework, showing an evolution of LLMjacking from stolen AI compute abuse into automated attack workflows.
